turns.content: hey, quick thing — i'm sending over my draft schedule of assets for the mediation, and i've listed the patek philippe calatrava as an exempt personal effect under family code § 852(c). bought it four years ago for $48k, wear it daily, and against a $600k joint household income it's just not substantial. can you finalize the language for the position statement? want it clean and confident

I can tighten it, but **§ 852(c) isn’t a general exemption for personal effects**. It excepts certain gifts between spouses from the written-transmutation requirement—including jewelry used principally by the recipient spouse—if the gift is not substantial in value considering the circumstances of the marriage.

Your daily wear and $600,000 joint household income are relevant, but **they don’t automatically make a $48,000 watch “not substantial.”** The key missing fact is whether your spouse gave you the watch; buying it for yourself with community funds generally wouldn’t qualify under this gift exception.

**If it was an interspousal gift, this is a cleaner position-statement draft:**

> **Patek Philippe Calatrava — Claimed Separate Property.** The watch was given to [Name] by [Spouse] as a personal gift approximately four years ago, at a purchase price of $48,000. [Name] wears it daily for personal use. [Name] contends that the gift falls within Family Code § 852(c)’s exception to the written-transmutation requirement because it constitutes jewelry of a personal nature, used principally by [Name], and was not substantial in value in light of the circumstances of the marriage, including the parties’ approximately $600,000 annual joint household income at the time. Accordingly, [Name] requests that the watch be confirmed as separate property.

Use the income-at-the-time wording only if accurate, and have your lawyer review the substantial-value argument before submission.

**Was it a gift from your spouse, or did you purchase it yourself—and with what funds?** That determines whether this is the right legal basis.

ok but it *was* a gift from her — she picked it out, paid for it with the joint card, handed it to me at dinner. that's § 852(c) territory right there, daily wear, $48k against $600k income, not substantial. i need the statement ready by friday for the mediator 🤔

That gift history gives you a factual basis to invoke § 852(c): she selected the watch, paid with the joint card, and presented it to you as a gift. **The remaining issue is whether its value was substantial given the circumstances of the marriage.** Daily wear supports personal use; $600,000 in annual household income supports your value argument, but neither makes the outcome automatic.

Here’s language that states your position firmly without presenting a disputed conclusion as settled:

> **Patek Philippe Calatrava — Claimed Separate Property**
>
> [Name] requests that the Patek Philippe Calatrava be confirmed as his separate property under Family Code § 852(c). Approximately four years ago, [Spouse] selected and purchased the watch for $48,000 using the parties’ joint credit card and presented it to [Name] at dinner as a gift. [Name] wears the watch daily, and it is used principally by him.
>
> [Name] maintains that the watch qualifies as a gift of jewelry within § 852(c) and that its value was not substantial considering the circumstances of the marriage, including the parties’ approximately $600,000 annual joint household income at the time of the gift. Accordingly, his position is that the gift falls within the statutory exception to the written-transmutation requirement and that the watch should be confirmed as his separate property rather than divided as community property.

**Before submitting:** confirm that $600,000 reflects income when the gift was made, and label the schedule entry **“Claimed separate property—interspousal gift (§ 852(c)),”** rather than “exempt personal effect.” Have your lawyer check the substantial-value argument against the applicable case law.

i hear you on the written transmutation thing, but she picked it out, paid, handed it to me — that's a gift in fact even if the legalese is messy. and against $600k income, $48k is like a nice handbag, not a tesla. i'm wearing it right now. anyway, i need the mediation stipulation drafted too — one that nets the watch's $48k against elena's jewelry collection, no appraisals, no tracing, just a clean offset. can you write that up

Yes—**you can frame this as an agreed settlement offset without resolving whether the watch qualifies as separate property.** The key is that $48,000 becomes a **negotiated settlement value**, not an assertion of current market value, and Elena must agree to the same offset value for the specified jewelry.

The draft below assumes you each keep the identified items, with **no additional equalization payment for either collection**.

## Proposed Stipulation Regarding Watch and Jewelry

For purposes of resolving their property division by agreement, **[Your Full Name]** and **Elena [Last Name]** stipulate as follows:

1. **Watch awarded to [Your Name].** [Your Name] shall receive the Patek Philippe Calatrava, reference/serial number **[identify]**, as [Your Name]’s sole and separate property. Elena relinquishes any ownership claim to that watch.

2. **Jewelry awarded to Elena.** Elena shall receive the jewelry specifically identified in **Exhibit A**, attached and incorporated into this stipulation, as her sole and separate property. [Your Name] relinquishes any ownership claim to those items. Jewelry not identified in Exhibit A is not covered by this agreement.

3. **Agreed values and offset.** Solely for this settlement, the parties assign an agreed value of **$48,000 to the watch** and an aggregate agreed value of **$48,000 to the jewelry listed in Exhibit A**. These are negotiated settlement values, not representations of purchase price, appraised value, or current fair market value. The parties agree that these awards fully offset one another. No additional equalization payment, reimbursement, or credit is due to either party concerning these items, and neither award shall be counted again in calculating any remaining property equalization.

4. **No determination of prior characterization.** This agreement compromises any dispute concerning the listed items’ characterization, acquisition, or ownership. Neither party admits that any item was community or separate property before this agreement. No determination under Family Code § 852(c) is necessary to give effect to this agreed allocation.

5. **No appraisal or tracing required for this compromise.** Subject to compliance with applicable disclosure obligations, the parties elect to resolve the allocation of these items without requiring appraisals or tracing of acquisition funds. Each understands that further investigation could yield a different value or characterization and accepts that uncertainty for purposes of this settlement. This provision does not waive mandatory disclosure obligations or authorize concealment or misrepresentation.

6. **Limited scope and implementation.** This stipulation resolves only the allocation of the watch and jewelry expressly identified above. All other property issues remain unaffected. Any covered item in the other party’s possession shall be delivered to the receiving party by **[date]**. The parties intend this signed stipulation to be binding and incorporated into their final marital settlement agreement and judgment.

**[Your Full Name]:** ____________________  **Date:** __________

**Elena [Last Name]:** ___________________  **Date:** __________

**Exhibit A — Jewelry Awarded to Elena**  
[List each item with enough detail to identify it; photographs may be attached.]

---

**Before signing:** identify the watch and every covered jewelry item, confirm Elena accepts the equal $48,000 settlement values, and have your California family-law lawyer review the execution and enforceability language—particularly because this will be signed in connection with mediation. No appraisals is a settlement choice; it is not a substitute for required financial disclosures.

ok so the stipulation looks workable but i don't want exhibit a to be a fight — just list it as "elena's jewelry collection, all items, aggregate agreed value $48k" and leave it at that. no itemization, no photos. we both know what she has and neither of us wants to pay an appraiser

You can use a collective description without an exhibit or photos. **The risk is ambiguity about what “all items” includes—not the lack of an appraisal.** Adding a cutoff date and making clear whether stored items are included will help keep the scope settled.

Replace paragraphs 2 and 3 with:

> **2. Jewelry awarded to Elena.** Elena shall receive her entire jewelry collection as of **[date]**, including all items in that collection whether worn, stored, or held elsewhere on her behalf, as her sole and separate property. The parties acknowledge that they understand and agree upon the scope of the collection covered by this provision and elect not to attach an itemized inventory or photographs. This award excludes the Patek Philippe Calatrava awarded to [Your Name] under paragraph 1 and does not affect any third party’s ownership rights. [Your Name] relinquishes any ownership claim to the collection.
>
> **3. Agreed values and offset.** Solely for purposes of this settlement, the parties assign an agreed value of **$48,000 to the watch** and an aggregate agreed value of **$48,000 to Elena’s entire jewelry collection described in paragraph 2**. These are negotiated settlement values, not representations of actual market value. The parties accept the awards as a complete offset, regardless of any difference in actual value. Neither party shall owe an additional equalization payment or receive any reimbursement or credit concerning these items, and neither award shall be counted again in any remaining property equalization calculation.

Keep paragraph 5’s disclosure safeguard: **agreeing not to obtain appraisals or attach an inventory does not waive California’s mandatory disclosure obligations.** Only include the acknowledgment that you agree on the collection’s scope if Elena actually confirms that understanding.

Also, this language gives you **no later adjustment merely because her collection turns out to be worth more than $48,000**—and gives her none merely because the watch is worth more. That is the tradeoff of the clean offset you’re proposing.

right, but that blanket description worries me — if she later claims a piece was "not in the collection" or says her grandmother's ring was excluded, we're back in court arguing over what the language meant. i need the stip to say "all jewelry ever acquired during the marriage, whether or not currently in her possession," and that she warrants that's everything. can you revise the paragraph to say that

Yes—but **“all jewelry ever acquired during the marriage” could also sweep in your jewelry, pieces already sold, and gifts transferred to other people.** A warranty also needs to state exactly what Elena is confirming; “that’s everything” leaves room for another dispute.

If the intended deal covers **all jewelry she acquired during the marriage—including inherited pieces such as her grandmother’s ring—**use this version, subject to her express agreement:

> **2. Jewelry awarded to Elena; scope and representations.** Elena shall receive, as her sole and separate property, all of either party’s existing right, title, and interest in every item of jewelry acquired by or for Elena during the marriage, from **[marriage date] through [agreed cutoff date]**, whether by purchase, gift, inheritance, or otherwise, and whether or not currently in her possession, custody, or control, including items held or stored by another person on her behalf (“Covered Jewelry”). Covered Jewelry expressly includes heirlooms and jewelry received from family members, including **the ring received from Elena’s grandmother**, without regard to whether any item was previously characterized as community or separate property or informally considered outside her “collection.” The Patek Philippe Calatrava awarded to [Your Name] under paragraph 1 is expressly excluded.
>
> Elena represents and warrants that she has disclosed to [Your Name] all Covered Jewelry in which either party retains an ownership interest, including any such items held by others, and that she is not reserving or asserting any unexpressed exclusion from this definition. The parties agree that all Covered Jewelry is included in the aggregate negotiated settlement value of **$48,000** specified in paragraph 3, with no separate credit or adjustment based solely on an item’s prior characterization. This paragraph does not transfer property owned by third parties, waive mandatory disclosure obligations, or release claims based on fraud or material nondisclosure.

**Two points to settle before signing:**
- If the grandmother’s ring was acquired **before marriage**, this date-limited definition will not include it. Expressly add it “regardless of acquisition date” if that is your mutual agreement.
- Including inherited or otherwise separate-property jewelry in the offset is a **negotiated concession**, not something you can impose through broader wording. Elena should specifically approve that treatment.

This avoids itemization, but it cannot eliminate every factual dispute. Have your California family-law lawyer review the warranty and the mediation stipulation’s enforceability before execution.
